definition: Tonal sensation is the conscious hearing of a tone or sound-pitch. In the historical example given, it is the auditory experience produced by a tuning fork and may fade from awareness even while the physical stimulation is still being considered.

reasons: The second sentence adds an unsupported claim: the packet’s tuning-fork example only says the tonal sensation can cease and a faint tone may later return; it does not say the experience fades while the physical stimulation is still being considered.

The definition slightly overstates the sense by presenting it as simply the conscious hearing of a tone or sound-pitch; the packet frames this as an experimental example of a tonal sensation in a historical psychology text, not a general settled definition.
The packet does not define “tonal sensation” as “the conscious hearing of a tone or sound-pitch.” It only mentions the phrase in connection with Fechner’s experiment using a tuning-fork.

The packet does not state that tonal sensation “may fade from awareness even while the physical stimulation is still being considered.” It only describes that the tonal sensation has entirely ceased before removing the fork, followed by hearing a faint tone when the fork is brought to the ear again.
The definition’s first sentence contains substantive explanatory claims not supported anywhere in the provided packet text.
